articles.title: Reading a tide table in ten minutes
articles.abstract: A short guide to the columns of a coastal tide table and what they mean for a day on the water.
articles.text:
A tide table lists the time and height of each high and low water for one port.

Read the day first, then the height. Subtract the height of low water from the next high water to get the range, and plan the crossing around the hour when the range is smallest.

articles.title: Why ferry timetables slip in winter
articles.abstract: Four small causes of winter delays on short coastal ferry routes, from tides to crew rotas.
articles.text:
Winter timetables carry less slack. A ferry that turns around in twelve minutes in July needs twenty when the quay is wet.

Crew rotas add a second effect: one late arrival moves every later sailing.

articles.title: What a small harbour charges and why
articles.abstract: A plain-language walk through mooring, berthing and water fees at a small working harbour.
articles.text:
Harbour fees fall into three groups: a charge for the space, a charge for services, and a charge for the time.

The space charge follows the length of the boat. Services such as water and power are metered. Time is usually per night, with a lower weekly rate.

articles.title: A notebook of six working knots
articles.abstract: Six knots a small-boat sailor uses weekly, with the one mistake that spoils each.
articles.text:
The bowline, the clove hitch, the figure eight, the sheet bend, the round turn and two half hitches, and the rolling hitch.

Each fails the same way: it is tied once, quickly, and never checked under load.

articles.title: The dock that was never finished
articles.abstract: A short history of an invented dock scheme, and what its unfinished quay still tells the town.
articles.text:
The scheme was approved in a wet spring and abandoned by the autumn.

What remains is a quay that stops in mid-air, used now by anglers and by the town on festival days.

articles.title: Weather notes for the shoulder season (draft)
articles.abstract: A draft set of notes on reading a falling barometer in spring and autumn.
articles.text:
A barometer that falls three millibars in three hours is a warning, not a forecast.

Combine it with the wind shift before deciding to leave the mooring.

articles.title: An allotment diary for a cold March
articles.abstract: Week-by-week notes from an invented allotment on what to sow under cover and what to leave alone.
articles.text:
Week one: sow nothing outdoors. Start leeks and onions in trays on a window sill.

Week three: the soil is still below six degrees; leave the carrots.

articles.title: How a village bus route is saved
articles.abstract: A case study of an invented rural bus route kept alive by a parish scheme.
articles.text:
The route carried eleven passengers a day and cost more than it earned.

The parish bought the Tuesday and Friday runs, and the operator kept the rest.
